Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a failed Swedish book publisher who decides to take a train from Stockholm to Berlin. Unfortunately for everyone around him, he's a walking disaster, causing mayhem everywhere he goes. The train also holds a man and his lover who plan to murder the man's wife (who is also on the train), a soldier on his way home, two gay elderly gentlemen, an angry train conductor, two nuns, a group of students, and even more characters. Meant as a mix of coming-of-age drama (which it tries to be - at least to begin with) and comedy, the film fails with both. It doesn't feel right as the tone changes multiple times every few minutes, and as the train races towards its final destination, the film becomes more and more bizarre, with very few truly funny moments remaining. The few good bits are lost in a myriad of pointless plots and characters. The cast itself is packed with famous Swedish actors, no matter how small their roles are. It's like the director called everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part in the film. Too bad, their performances are just as bad as the script (actress lines are often written for men). The comedy is more slap than slapstick, with the same jokes repeated over and over. The pacing is incredibly slow at times (quite often, actually), with on scene in particular dragging on for over ten minutes for no good reason. The screenwriter also seems to think that swearing is a good way to replace good dialogue. The film has some nice visuals in moody B&W, but it's wasted on such inept film-making in every other way. [2/5]

This rather silly romantic comedy is based on the kind of story I loved as a teenager, but now find rather ridiculous. It's about the idea of inter-age romantic attachments, where whatever is on the mind of the elder person is either lust, or an attempt to escape the reality of aging, or both. And the younger person is usually looking for the kind parent that she (or he) lacked as a child. These stories now seem more pathetic than funny to me, but there is also something rather nostalgic about them. Dick Powell looked a bit embarrassed--as perhaps he should have--as the elder lover in this romantic comedy. He was, at fifty, playing the part of a thirty-eight-year-old man romancing a teen-ager. But young Debbie Reynolds was a revelation--sweet and saucy, honey and vinegar--as a beautiful, innocent sixteen-year-old hired as a model by "The Author," the morally bankrupt and cynical screenwriter, as a subject for him to study. Her spirited performance alone earns from me a better rating than the film might otherwise deserve. Anne Baxter is cast as Powell's beautiful, but shallow fiancée, and handles her small part deftly. Some of the dialogue is quite amusing, too, so it's not a total washout. 5/6

I have no idea how accurate the portrayal of Flynn appears in this film, but as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The plot is all over the place and leaves you wondering how you got from one scene to the next. There are just too many twists and turns needed to keep track of Flynn and his current situation, and it is difficult to understand Flynn's and other characters' motivations for some of their behaviour. Add to that a series of silly and implausible events and you have something that comes across like one of your dreams that seems to make sense while you are asleep, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is just strange, confusing, and completely unrealistic. There are many long and boring musical sections in the film that to me look like poor direction or a bad director, and not like any artistic choice. All the characters are one-dimensional, especially Flynn, who comes across as a self serving jerk, thug, thief, robber, murderer, liar, gambler, gigolo, and drug addict who will do anything and step on anyone to advance his own interests, but somehow, despite all that, great opportunities always seem to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining or satisfying in any way and by all accounts not even well made, so I would avoid it. To rub salt in the wound, the DVD was one of the worst transfers I have ever seen, it wasn't even in wide-screen or Dolby 5.1, it had a poor, quality, and many scratches and artifacts from what looked like a film reel that had been gathering dust somewhere..

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is generally maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as mentally bridging some of the jump cuts in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

See, the first act of the film is spent establishing nuances of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his aggression is delivered within minutes of the first title cards. As for the narration and many of the flashbacks: needless. The pacing during the second act was tedious. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger eating, then vomiting, then eating some more, then flailing his arms and saying something snappy or rude. All the while, the schlock is punctuated with brief scenes of Jack discussing his rage problems with a therapist. (Definitely the entertaining scenes in the film -- excellent dialog worth plenty of laughs.) Then, without warning, Jack decides to kill a few monsters. And then it's over. All in all, as a throwback to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has loads of potential but is purposeless and plods on without conflict or adequate resolution. Hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks VII: Jack Goes to Hell or Jack vs. Ash go into production.

This movie is based on the series Street Fighter Alpha (or Zero)! It is placed in an other setting than Streetfighter the animated movie! This movie is all about Ryu who is accompanied by Ken and Chun Li. I recognized Rose,Zanghief and Birdie! There weren't any other characters used from the video game (that i could discover)! The fighting scenes were OK but nothing really spectacular! And there were not many of them! To me this is odd! Isn't Streetfighter about fighting! Streetfighter the animated movie (1994) is far superior to this movie. It tries to be more than it really is! The use of the "Hada Power" and other supernatural elemnents have nothing to do with skills the characters have in the video game! And in this case that is a bad thing! The story is so boring that you don't really care what is happening! The action is toned down considerably! Why? And what happened to the other characters from the video game! Surely they are more interesting than the villain in this story! The main attraction of the video game are the characters with their own special skills! In this movie it is all about Ryu! That is why this anime fails!

This movie is based on the game Streetfighter II (or III)! It is placed in an alternate setting from Streetfighter II animated movie! This movie is all about Ryu who is accompanied by Ken and Chun-Li I think also,Zanghief and Sagat! There weren't any other characters used from the video game (that i know of)! The fighting scenes are OK but not really exciting! And there aren't many of them! I find this movie odd because the classic Streetfighter II fighting from Streetfighter II animated movie (1994) is not present in this movie. This movie has a fighting of it's own with the use of the "R Dragon Kick" and other new fighting moves that have nothing to do with what the characters have in the video game! And in this case that is a bad thing! The story is also boring and you don't really care what is happening! The action is slowed down considerably! You also wonder what happened to the other characters from the video game! Surely they didn't become the main villain in this movie! The main point of the video game was the characters with their own special skills! In this movie it is all about Ryu! That is why this anime fails
